profile.name: Pursere Kattuna
profile.tagline: A nocturnal ritual folk dance of Tulunadu blessing homes with healing and mythic farce.
profile.insight: From late evening until the early hours of the morning, dancers visit village homes in Belthangady, embodying characters from wild animals to ascetics.
profile.profile: Pursere Kattuna is a religious and traditional folk dance form of Tulunadu, performed mainly in Belthangady taluk during the full moon in the month of Suggi. The nocturnal ritual spans from late evening to early morning, featuring acting, singing, dancing, and mythological mimicry to bless homes with healing and prosperity. Initiated mainly by the Tulu Gowda community, it draws on the Natha Pantha spiritual tradition and involves diverse characters ranging from priests and Koti Chennaya to wild animals and ghosts.
profile.profile_long:
Pursere Kattuna stands as a religious and traditional folk dance form deeply rooted in the cultural landscape of Tulunadu. Performed primarily within the villages of Belthangady taluk situated in the Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, India, this tradition is carried out by Tulu-speaking people hailing from various castes and backgrounds. The timing of the performance is strictly observed, taking place during the auspicious full moon in the month of Suggi according to the traditional Tulu calendar. This nocturnal event commences in the late evening and continues uninterrupted until the early hours of the morning, enveloping the community in a continuous wave of ritual action.

As the night unfolds, the performance encompasses a rich tapestry of acting, singing, dancing, symbolic storytelling, and mythological mimicry. Dancers travel directly to the homes of community members belonging to different social strata. Upon arrival, they bless the households and their inhabitants with healing, prosperity, and protection. Throughout the various stages of the enactment, performers maintain an active dialogue and interaction, engaging both with one another and with the gathered public. This communal framework is heavily influenced by the Natha Pantha spiritual tradition, infusing the theatrical display with deep devotional resonance. Individuals step into distinct roles and embody diverse characters, sustaining the energy of the event throughout the dark hours until dawn breaks over the village.

The visual presentation of Pursere Kattuna relies upon an extensive range of costumes and assigned roles that represent a broad cross-section of castes, professions, mythic figures, and social archetypes. Performers don attire depicting Brahmins and priests, mendicants, ascetics, and fortune tellers, as well as legendary figures such as Koti Chennaya. The cast also features wild animals including bears, tigers, lions, and monkeys, alongside scholars, thieves, ghosts, and other spiritual entities. Further broadening the social scope of the performance are a Christian male character and a Muslim female character, alongside farcical figures designed to challenge, provoke, and entertain through humor, mimicry, and social satire. Although the performances are initiated primarily by the Tulu Gowda community, individuals from diverse other communities join in freely to participate. A closely related type of performance exists in the nearby Sullia region, distinguished by a different costume style known as Siddavesha, which highlights three notable mythic farce characters: Sanyasi, Bhatru, and Dasayye.

The auditory and rhythmic foundation of Pursere Kattuna is provided by a specific ensemble of traditional musical instruments. The ensemble includes the Tase, the Dolu, the Nadaswara, and the Shruti. These instruments play a critical role in guiding the rhythm of the dance, supporting the delivery of mythic dialogues, and sustaining the continuous sequence of singing that reverberates throughout the night. The percussive drive of the drums combined with the sustained tones of the wind and drone instruments creates a soundscape that unifies the various theatrical elements.

Ultimately, Pursere Kattuna functions as a cornerstone of living heritage in Tulunadu. It seamlessly combines ritual healing, traditional belief systems, humor, performance art, and community theatre into an integrated cultural expression. By bringing these elements to life year after year, the tradition brilliantly showcases the vibrant folk imagination of Tulu society while ensuring the preservation of oral narratives, intricate mythic storytelling, and vital seasonal practices for future generations.

sections.origins_and_history: Pursere Kattuna is a religious and traditional folk dance form of Tulunadu, performed mainly in the villages of Belthangady taluk in the Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, India, by Tulu-speaking people from various castes. The style shows influence from the Natha Pantha spiritual tradition.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance takes place from late evening until the early hours of the morning during the full moon in the month of Suggi. Dancers visit homes of different social strata, engaging in acting, singing, dancing, symbolic storytelling, and mythological mimicry while interacting with each other and the public.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical accompaniment is provided by instruments including the Tase, Dolu, Nadaswara, and Shruti, which guide the rhythm of the dance, mythic dialogues, and singing sequences throughout the night.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes represent diverse roles such as Brahmins, priests, mendicants, ascetics, fortune tellers, Koti Chennaya, wild animals (bears, tigers, lions, monkeys), scholars, thieves, ghosts, spiritual entities, a Christian male, a Muslim female, and farcical characters. A similar performance in Sullia uses the Siddavesha costume style featuring Sanyasi, Bhatru, and Dasayye.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Held during the full moon in the Suggi month, the ritual blesses homes with healing, prosperity, and protection. It combines ritual healing, traditional belief, humor, performance art, and community theatre, preserving oral narratives and mythic storytelling.
sections.regional_variants: A similar type of performance exists in the Sullia region using a different costume style known as Siddavesha, featuring mythic farce characters Sanyasi, Bhatru, and Dasayye.
sections.lineage: Influenced by the Natha Pantha spiritual tradition.
